takeaways.title: Cybersecurity is several different jobs.
takeaways.text: A scanner finds candidate problems. A pentest investigates weaknesses. A red team tests defensive response. A managed provider operates agreed controls. Knowing which question you are paying to answer matters more than comparing feature lists.

takeaways.title: The handoffs are where meaning changes.
takeaways.text: A request becomes a saved capture, a capture becomes a finding, and a finding becomes a report. Identity, missing data, filters and serialization can change what survives. The research follows those handoffs in real source code.

takeaways.title: A successful command is only one step.
takeaways.text: A job can complete while work continues. An isolation request can be accepted before a device is isolated. A finding can disappear from a report without the weakness being repaired. Check the actual effect.

takeaways.title: AI needs the same evidence discipline.
takeaways.text: Agents can help investigate and coordinate tools, but a persuasive explanation or benchmark score does not prove a customer system is secure. Permissions, inputs, recovery and independent checks remain central.

tracks.title: Who the security companies are, and how they work
tracks.researched: Ten representative providers with Japan relevance, plus a separate GMO Flatt Security supplement: their history, finances, products, managed services, onboarding, incident response and specific AI features.
tracks.learn: Understand what CrowdStrike, Microsoft, Google/Mandiant, Palo Alto, Fortinet, Cisco/Splunk, Trend Micro, LAC, NRI Secure and GMO Ierae actually supply—and where the customer still makes decisions.
tracks.example: Requesting endpoint isolation, receiving an API result and verifying containment are separate stages. Approval and operating responsibilities vary by service and contract.
tracks.limit: Public documents and selected public code establish documented mechanisms, not independent effectiveness or undisclosed internal operations. This is a representative sample, not a top-ten ranking.

tracks.title: What assessments do, and how testing engines work
tracks.researched: Red teaming, pentesting, ethical hacking, assessment providers and standards; NBRET's existing capabilities; source paths in ZAP, Nuclei, garak and PentestGPT; isolated known-answer experiments.
tracks.learn: Choose the right assessment for a question, understand what a finding means, and see why an HTTP status or scanner alert alone can be misleading.
tracks.example: The tenant-disclosure fixture demonstrates why checking only a status code misses the intended security property. You need to check who received which data, under which identity.
tracks.limit: Synthetic fixtures establish their specific outcomes. Wider discovery ability, real identity integrations and complete runtime coverage remain open; proposed product ideas are hypotheses.

tracks.title: How the tools see networks, requests and identities
tracks.researched: VPNs, proxies and tunnels; Nmap discovery; mitmproxy request and saved-flow behavior; packet decoding; identity collection and graph analysis; cloud posture and reporting/retest workflows.
tracks.learn: Follow one observation from the network into an analyst's report. Understand which tool supplies a path, which records traffic, and which interprets permissions.
tracks.example: A proxy's saved flow can differ from what was forwarded, and a reporting system can close a finding because it disappeared on reimport. Neither alone establishes the original bytes or a verified fix.
tracks.limit: Selected loopback and mocked tests complement pinned source reads. They do not establish enterprise coverage; proprietary Burp internals and many native runtime paths were not inspected or executed.

tracks.title: How bots and workers coordinate real work
tracks.researched: Bot identity, rate-limit keys, queues, worker locks, leases, retries, cancellation, scheduling and database-adapter boundaries across selected implementations.
tracks.learn: Reason about shared IPs versus individual identities, duplicated work, retries and what it takes to stop a running task.
tracks.example: In the controlled limiter fixture, IP-based keys wrongly group different principals and miss one principal changing address labels. In the adapted worker check, cancellation signals the processor; an ignoring processor can keep running.
tracks.limit: Those are finite fixture and adapted-class outcomes. Toy scheduling and mocked dependencies are labelled separately from real broker or database integration.

tracks.title: How to tell whether a security claim is justified
tracks.status: Active investigation; substantial accessible work remains
tracks.researched: Incident chains, assessment quality, approval states, executable claims, AI-agent recovery and memory, evaluation oracles, permission resolution and evidence transformations in selected pinned projects.
tracks.learn: Read a test or report critically: what was checked, what counted as success, what was substituted, and whether the result supports the claimed outcome.
tracks.example: An agent's trace or exact quoted evidence can support where a claim came from. It still needs a meaningful check of the claim and a separate boundary enforcing what the agent may do.
tracks.limit: Source-established behavior, synthetic execution, authored tests, failures and proposals remain distinct. There is no customer-environment validation; stopped operations remain stopped.
